newsitem.title: USA: With Russia in G7, can China be far behind?.
newsitem.headline: With Russia in G7, can China be far behind?.

text.p: With Russia assuming a prominent new place at the annual summit of the world's major industrialised nations, the absence of China, an economic giant with a nuclear arsenal, is all the more pronounced.
That is not likely to change soon, although some analysts, including U.S. officials, believe increasingly that excluding Beijing is a serious mistake.

"The problem with the G7 or G8 is that it rarely corresponds to the seven or eight countries you most want in the room" when discussing key issues, said Richard Haass, a former Bush adminstration official who now directs foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution.

"It doesn't include the two most populous countries in the world -- China and India, both of which have booming economies. It's something of a holdover from the previous era when the United States and a handful of countries in Europe and Japan dominated. While it may be useful on some issues, it clearly is not the ideal grouping for most," he told Reuters.
Russia has been edging toward acceptance in the Group of Seven or G7 -- the exclusive club of the world's richest countries -- since just before the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.

As the former communist superpower began evolving toward a free market democracy, a common denominator of all G7 members, the United States and its partners -- France, Germany, Italy, Canada, Japan and Britain -- allowed Moscow to participate on the margins of their political discussions.
But at their annual meeting set for June 20-22 in Denver, Colorado, now called the "summit of the eight," Russia will play a larger role while stopping short of full membership.
This resulted from a deal forged at a March U.S.-Russia summit in Helsinki that is tied to U.S. efforts to assuage Moscow's concerns over NATO expansion into eastern Europe.
U.S. officials say there has been no serious talk in the government about inviting China to join the G7. Rather, attention has been focused on Russia.
Also, despite an intensified American effort to engage with China, tensions remain over Beijing's huge trade surplus, human rights, arm sales, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
President Bill Clinton's decision to renew Most Favoured Nation trade status for China, moreover, has provoked some members of Congress to fight to overturn his MFN designation.

Although its economy is burgeoning, China's gross national product is $560 billion versus $1.1 trillion for Russia, $1 trillion for Italy and $571 billion for Canada, according to the latest (1995) figures published by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London.

But the Heritage Foundation, a conservative thinktank, says in its annual "index of economic freedom" worldwide that there is little difference between Russia and China -- both economies are "mostly not free" when rated according to trade and tax policies and other factors.
While Beijing will not be sitting at the table in Denver, it will be on the minds of summit participants.

U.S. officials said Hong Kong is likely to be on the agenda with Washington pushing for endorsement of its view that the British colony should retain maximum political and economic freedoms when it reverts to China's control after June 30.
Apart from specific concerns, China differs from other summit of the eight members in that it is not a democracy.

Experts Richard Bernstein and Ross Munro write in a recent Foreign Affairs magazine that "while the forces pushing toward global democracy are probably too powerful for China to remain unaffected by them forever, there is no reason to believe China will become democratic in the near future" in part because that runs counter to China's 3,000-year-old history.
Despite all this, Haass insists the G7 is becoming an anachronism and either must be altered or scrapped.
"It's hard to argue that Italy and Canada are more important in managing international affiars than China or India, or Brazil and South Africa," he said.

He expects if the summit remains a viable grouping -- and some influential U.S. officials insist it is essential the G7 meet to take decisions on economic matters -- then "China will be invited in after it joins the World Trade Organisation."
But the smarter approach would be to "move away from this formal annual event and instead have meetings when you need them with the countries you need," Haass says.

At least some U.S. officials also would include China in the annual summit. "It would be terrific to have them in. China is always complaining they are left out of major institutions. This would increase their obligations to behave," one official told Reuters.
